main.title: Guild Wars 2
main.subtitle: An online world built around spontaneous cooperation
main.summary: ArenaNet launched Guild Wars 2 on August 28, 2012, with dynamic events, active combat and no mandatory monthly subscription.

cards.heading: An online world built around spontaneous cooperation
cards.text: ArenaNet officially launched Guild Wars 2 on August 28, 2012. Pre-purchase and pre-order customers had earlier headstart periods, which the studio distinguished from the formal launch. Its online world emphasizes dynamic events, exploration and cooperation between players. Participation does not require being the first player to attack an enemy, and exploration provides rewards across the landscape.

cards.heading: Joining dynamic events without forming a party
cards.text: In many areas, events begin in the shared world: a village is attacked, a caravan needs an escort, or a creature changes the state of a zone. Nearby players can participate without first forming a party or accepting the same quest. These events encourage spontaneous cooperation rather than making players compete for the same resource, although they do not remove the repetition common to MMOs.

cards.heading: Dodging and changing skills through weapons
cards.text: Position matters in Guild Wars 2 combat. Dodging consumes a resource, many abilities create visible areas of effect, and equipped weapons change part of the available skill set. Players must move during encounters rather than only between targets. The system supports roles and synergies without forcing every encounter into a rigid division between tank, healer and damage dealer.

cards.heading: A complete game without a monthly subscription
cards.text: At launch, Guild Wars 2 was sold as a complete product without a mandatory monthly subscription. Players could leave for several weeks and return without paying for unused subscription time. ArenaNet combined this business model with a world designed for casual cooperation. Later updates repeatedly changed the structure of the game.

main.title: HarmoKnight
main.subtitle: A platform game follows the score
main.summary: HarmoKnight is Game Freak's Nintendo 3DS rhythm platformer about Tempo, a young hero travelling through the musical world of Melodia. Automatically scrolling stages ask him to jump and swing a staff in time with the soundtrack. Enemies and percussion plants become opportunities to add notes to a performance. The simple controls make the connection between music and movement immediately readable. A successful run looks like a small adventure, but its obstacles have been placed so that the player's physical actions can also complete the rhythm of the scene.

cards.heading: A platform game follows the score
cards.text: HarmoKnight is Game Freak's Nintendo 3DS rhythm platformer about Tempo, a young hero travelling through the musical world of Melodia. Automatically scrolling stages ask him to jump and swing a staff in time with the soundtrack. Enemies and percussion plants become opportunities to add notes to a performance. The simple controls make the connection between music and movement immediately readable. A successful run looks like a small adventure, but its obstacles have been placed so that the player's physical actions can also complete the rhythm of the scene.

cards.heading: Two buttons, several musical demands
cards.text: Jumping and striking use separate buttons, with the staff also able to charge for a stronger note-earning hit. Routes can contain optional targets and hidden bonuses, giving a skilled player reasons to do more than reach the exit safely. Some stages use different time signatures or changes in speed, asking the hand to adjust to what is heard. The controls remain stable while the musical context changes. That makes a familiar action difficult in another way: the question becomes when to perform it, and how to preserve the phrase through the next obstacle.

cards.heading: The best run opens a faster one
cards.text: Collected notes determine the grade at the end of a stage, and a strong result unlocks a faster version. Boss encounters ask Tempo to answer sequences of actions, while other sections introduce companions with different ways to engage with the music. Bonus stages also use Pokémon melodies, connecting Game Freak's experiment to its better-known work. HarmoKnight builds progression around improved listening. A route first learned as a line of visible hazards can eventually be recognised as a musical pattern, with another speed offering a fresh test of that understanding.

main.title: Mark of the Ninja
main.subtitle: Klei brings stealth to a side-scrolling platform game
main.summary: Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling stealth platform game developed by Klei Entertainment and published by Microsoft Studios.

cards.heading: Klei brings stealth to a side-scrolling platform game
cards.text: Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling stealth platform game developed by Klei Entertainment and published by Microsoft Studios. It was announced on February 28, 2012, and later released for the Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade on September 7, 2012. The game was released for Microsoft Windows on October 16, 2012, and for Linux and OS X on September 11, 2013. A remastered version was released on October 9, 2018, for Xbox One, PlayStation 4, Nintendo Switch, Microsoft Windows, macOS, and Linux by Klei Entertainment.

cards.heading: Ninja tradition meets modern technology
cards.text: The game follows the story of a nameless ninja in the present day, and features a conflict between ancient ninja tradition and modern technology. Cutscenes for the game are rendered in a Saturday-morning cartoon animation style.

cards.heading: Making light, sound and sight readable
cards.text: Mark of the Ninja consists of stealth-oriented 2D platforming. The character is required to sneak through a series of environments while staying out of sight of guards and performing silent assassinations. Levels are divided into areas of light and darkness; the player character is visible to enemies in the former and invisible in the latter, though passing within a certain immediate distance of an enemy's face results in the player being spotted irrespective of lighting. Sounds such as running may also give away the player character's location and are represented visually by a rapidly expanding circle. Unusual for a platformer, Mark of the Ninja employs a line of sight mechanic, meaning that enemies which would be invisible to the character are also invisible to the player, though their sounds are represented on screen in the same manner as the player character's.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim for atmosphere and stealth
cards.text: Mark of the Ninja received critical acclaim, with reviewers praising the game's visual and audio atmosphere, strong gameplay, and new take on the stealth genre, though some criticized its control scheme and difficult puzzles.

main.title: FTL: Faster Than Light
main.subtitle: A crew, a ship and a pursuing fleet
main.summary: FTL: Faster Than Light is a roguelike game created by indie developer Subset Games, which was released for Windows, MacOS, and Linux in September 2012.

cards.heading: A crew, a ship and a pursuing fleet
cards.text: FTL: Faster Than Light is a roguelike game created by indie developer Subset Games, which was released for Windows, MacOS, and Linux in September 2012. In the game, the player controls the crew of a single spacecraft, holding critical information to be delivered to an allied fleet, while being pursued by a large rebel fleet. The player must guide the spacecraft through eight sectors, each with planetary systems and events procedurally generated in a roguelike fashion, while facing rebel and other hostile forces, recruiting new crew, and outfitting and upgrading their ship. Combat takes place in pausable real time, and if the ship is destroyed or all of its crew lost, the game ends, forcing the player to restart with a new ship.

cards.heading: Every system can become an emergency
cards.text: Jump points can lead to stores, distress calls, hostile ships or other events. Combat runs in real time but can be paused to assign crew, redistribute power and choose targets. Damage may disable systems, start fires or breach the hull, forcing the crew to repair while the fight continues. Victories supply scrap and other resources for upgrades. When the engines charge, either ship may attempt to escape.

cards.heading: Two developers build a starship command game
cards.text: Subset Games began as the two-person team of Matthew Davis and Jay Ma, former colleagues at 2K's Shanghai studio. After leaving the studio in 2011, they agreed to spend a year developing FTL before deciding whether to continue independently. Its success allowed them to begin another project, Into the Breach.

main.title: Borderlands 2
main.subtitle: Gearbox returns to Pandora with four-player cooperation
main.summary: Borderlands 2 combines first-person shooting, character progression and loot in a cooperative adventure on Pandora.

cards.heading: Gearbox returns to Pandora with four-player cooperation
cards.text: Borderlands 2 launched in North America on September 18, 2012, followed by Europe on September 21. Gearbox returned to the first game's blend of first-person shooting and role-playing on Pandora, with distinct character classes, character progression and cooperation for up to four players. Loot remains central, while weapons and character abilities provide different ways to approach a battle.

cards.heading: Finding weapons with different behavior
cards.text: A weapon's value does not depend only on its statistics. Manufacturer, fire rate, accuracy, elemental effects and projectile behavior can suggest different distances and targets. Players compare newly found weapons with their current equipment and test how they work alongside character abilities. These differences make procedural variety noticeable during combat rather than only on a weapon's stat card.

cards.heading: Character roles and reviving allies
cards.text: Character abilities create specializations that are especially useful in a group. One companion can draw enemy attention while another controls a target or helps during a difficult phase. Players can also revive fallen allies. Different roles allow spontaneous coordination, and recovering a teammate can restore an important ability to the group.

cards.heading: Handsome Jack stays present through his voice
cards.text: Handsome Jack frequently comments and provokes through his voice without appearing physically in front of the player. His repeated interventions connect activities across Pandora and keep the main conflict present between side quests. The character combines self-justification and cruelty, commenting on events while the player is occupied elsewhere.

main.title: LittleBigPlanet PS Vita
main.subtitle: Sackboy brings play and creation to Vita
main.summary: LittleBigPlanet PS Vita is a 2012 puzzle-platform video game developed by Tarsier Studios and Double Eleven and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita.

cards.heading: Sackboy brings play and creation to Vita
cards.text: LittleBigPlanet PS Vita is a 2012 puzzle-platform video game developed by Tarsier Studios and Double Eleven and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita. It is the fourth main instalment of the LittleBigPlanet series. The game was announced in January 2011 along with the reveal of the PlayStation Vita console, then known as the Next Generation Portable (NGP), and the first details of the game were revealed on 6 June 2011 at the Electronic Entertainment Expo. It was released on 19 September 2012 in Europe, 20 September 2012 in Japan and Australia, and 25 September 2012 for the North American markets.

cards.heading: Touch controls reshape the platforming
cards.text: As in previous titles in the LittleBigPlanet series, players control a character named Sackboy through a variety of worlds utilising the character's various abilities such as jumping and grabbing objects. It also features various non-platforming mini-games. Numerous multiplayer options are available. As well as up to four-player online competitive or co-op gameplay, the PlayStation Vita's multi-touch display can be used by two players for competitive games. "Pass'n'Play" is also available, enabling turn-based gameplay. The Vita's rear touchpanel is also used for pushing objects toward the player, creating platforms out of parts of the world.

cards.heading: Players draw and share their own worlds
cards.text: Players are able to create their own levels and share them online using the PlayStation Network. The PlayStation Vita's touch-screen display can be used to directly draw objects and platforms in the game world. As well as unique creation tools such as these, the game also includes all of the tools available in LittleBigPlanet 2 (with the exception of its downloadable content tools such as the Wormhole). However, materials and stickers/decorations from prior games are not available in the game. Costumes bought from the PlayStation Network used to customise the player's character are transferable between the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita games, including LittleBigPlanet Karting, though costumes from the PSP game are not available in LittleBigPlanet PS Vita. Content can also be shared over both Wi-Fi and a 3G network.

main.title: DJMax Technika Tune
main.subtitle: An arcade music game moves under the fingers
main.summary: DJMax Technika Tune is Pentavision's PlayStation Vita rhythm game, first released in South Korea and Hong Kong on 20 September 2012. It adapts the touch-driven Technika arcade series to the handheld, using the front screen and rear touchpad to turn musical patterns into gestures. Notes appear across the playfield and must be activated in time with the moving musical sequence. The player is doing more than following a list of button prompts. The arrangement of touches becomes part of the performance, connecting rhythm to where a hand needs to move next.

cards.heading: An arcade music game moves under the fingers
cards.text: DJMax Technika Tune is Pentavision's PlayStation Vita rhythm game, first released in South Korea and Hong Kong on 20 September 2012. It adapts the touch-driven Technika arcade series to the handheld, using the front screen and rear touchpad to turn musical patterns into gestures. Notes appear across the playfield and must be activated in time with the moving musical sequence. The player is doing more than following a list of button prompts. The arrangement of touches becomes part of the performance, connecting rhythm to where a hand needs to move next.

cards.heading: Learn the pattern through touch
cards.text: Beginner modes simplify the charts, allowing the player to become comfortable with the timing before longer, repeated and chained notes are introduced. More demanding arrangements ask for coordinated movement across the screen and touchpad, giving familiar songs another level of physical complexity. Repeated play makes a pattern recognisable, so the next gesture can be prepared rather than improvised at the last moment. The handheld's surfaces give the arcade idea a new scale: a large cabinet interaction is condensed into something held directly in the player's hands without losing its emphasis on touching the music's visual structure.

cards.heading: A portable collection around the songs
cards.text: Producer Planetboom and designer XeoN led a release that also includes modes for listening to the soundtrack and watching its music videos. The North American edition contains sixty-seven tracks, giving the rhythm system a broad collection of charts to learn. Japan received the game in September 2012 and North America in December. Technika Tune belongs to the wider DJMax series but uses the Vita's particular hardware to establish its own play style. The result connects a specialised arcade tradition to a portable machine capable of making both sides of its body part of the input.

main.title: Resident Evil 6
main.subtitle: Four campaigns confront a worldwide bioterror attack
main.summary: Resident Evil 6 is a 2012 third-person shooter video game developed and published by Capcom.

cards.heading: Four campaigns confront a worldwide bioterror attack
cards.text: Resident Evil 6 is a 2012 third-person shooter video game developed and published by Capcom. It was released for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in October 2012, and for Windows in March 2013. It was re-released with all downloadable content for the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in March 2016, and for the Nintendo Switch in October 2019. Players control Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Jake Muller and Ada Wong as they confront the force behind a worldwide bio-terrorist attack. The story is centred around their four interwoven campaigns, and every campaign features a unique style in both tone and gameplay.

cards.heading: Partners, movement and campaign crossovers
cards.text: Leon, Chris and Jake each have a partner, controlled by another player or artificial intelligence. Ada's campaign later supports an additional Agent for cooperative play. New movement options include sliding, rolling and firing while moving. At crossover points, groups can meet online with up to four players. Quick-time events punctuate some encounters, while characters have distinct equipment and abilities.

cards.heading: Capcom builds its largest production
cards.text: Resident Evil 6 was conceived in 2009 and entered full development the following year under Resident Evil 4 producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi. It had a development staff of more than 600, making it Capcom's largest production.

cards.heading: Mixed reviews and a later return to survival horror
cards.text: Resident Evil 6 received mixed reviews from critics, who praised the graphics, artificial intelligence and controls, but criticized the execution of the interwoven campaigns and departure from the survival horror roots of the franchise in favor of a more action-oriented style. Despite these criticisms, the game sold 15.2 million units by September 2025. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, released in 2017, switched to a first-person perspective and returned to the survival horror genre.

main.title: Retro City Rampage
main.subtitle: An open city built from an eight-bit imagination
main.summary: Retro City Rampage is an action-adventure game developed by Vblank Entertainment. It is a parody of retro games and 1980s and 1990s pop culture, as well as Grand Theft Auto and similar games. It was first released for PlayStation 3, PlayStation Vita and Microsoft Windows in 2012, with ports later releasing for several other platforms.

cards.heading: A city of retro-game and pop-culture parodies
cards.text: Retro City Rampage is an action-adventure game developed by Vblank Entertainment. It is a parody of retro games and 1980s and 1990s pop culture, as well as Grand Theft Auto and similar games. It was first released for PlayStation 3, PlayStation Vita and Microsoft Windows in 2012, with ports later releasing for several other platforms.

cards.heading: An open city with changing perspectives
cards.text:
The game is inspired by Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto games, in that the player can complete a variety of missions within an enormous city that is open to explore. During development, around 50 story missions and 30 challenge levels were planned. Gameplay elements shared with GTA include the vast assortment of weaponry, the miscellaneous shops, the ability to hijack vehicles, and the ability to attract police attention with violence and destruction.

As a homage to numerous 8-bit video games, Retro City Rampage incorporates design elements from many different genres, and features 16 graphical filters that simulate various retro computers and game consoles. Although it is primarily played from a top-down bird's-eye viewpoint, in specific sections, it may switch to a strictly two-dimensional perspective in the style of a 2D platformer.

cards.heading: From Grand Theftendo to an original game
cards.text: Brian Provinciano began with Grand Theftendo, a homebrew attempt to recreate Grand Theft Auto III on NES hardware. Building his own development kit and tools taught him how to work within its limits. The project gradually gathered characters and places inspired by other childhood games, then became an original title in 2007 rather than a direct recreation. Moving development to PC removed the original hardware constraint, while a real-time map editor let him adjust and test the world as it grew. Playtesters' suggestions became another part of that process.

cards.heading: DX, an MS-DOS edition and a sequel
cards.text:
An enhanced version, Retro City Rampage DX, was released for Nintendo 3DS in 2014, followed by later ports for other platforms. Previous ports of the original version were later updated to the DX version via free updates. An MS-DOS version, Retro City Rampage 486, was released on July 29, 2015, as a limited physical run on a floppy disk as well as a free digital download for owners of the modern computer version of the game.

A sequel, Shakedown: Hawaii, was released in 2019.

main.title: XCOM: Enemy Unknown
main.subtitle: Firaxis reimagines the 1994 strategy game
main.summary: XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a 2012 turn-based tactics video game developed by Firaxis Games and published by 2K.

cards.heading: Firaxis reimagines the 1994 strategy game
cards.text: XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a 2012 turn-based tactics video game developed by Firaxis Games and published by 2K. It is a "reimagining" of the 1994 strategy game UFO: Enemy Unknown (also known as X-COM: UFO Defense). XCOM: Enemy Unknown is set during an alien invasion of Earth in an alternative version of 2015; the player controls an elite, multinational, paramilitary organization called XCOM and commands troops in a series of turn-based tactical missions. Between missions, the player directs the research and development of technologies from recovered alien technology and captured prisoners, expands XCOM's base of operations, manages finances, and monitors and responds to alien activity.

cards.heading: Jake Solomon and Sid Meier revisit the original design
cards.text: Firaxis attempted to reboot the franchise in 2003 but no product was marketed. Development of the game began in 2008 and lasted for four-and-a-half years. The game was initially envisioned as an exact remake of the 1994 game but the developers introduced improvements to gameplay mechanics and modernized the franchise. The development cycle was longer than those of other Firaxis games because it was retooled several times during production. Jake Solomon led development of the game, and studio head Sid Meier provided input and assisted the team. Aliens from the original game return in Enemy Unknown, though Firaxis redesigned many of them. While the game uses procedural generation for enemy placement, all maps in the game were handcrafted by Firaxis. Michael McCann composed the game's music.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim leads to an expansion and sequel
cards.text: XCOM: Enemy Unknown was announced in January 2012, and was released for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in October 2012. Handheld and mobile versions of the game, co-developed by 2K China, were later released. The game received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised the turn-based combat, presentation, emergent gameplay, difficulty and replayability but criticized its multiplayer component. It has since been considered as one of the greatest games of all time. It was a commercial success for the publisher and several gaming publications nominated it for year-end accolades, including Game of the Year. Firaxis released an expansion pack called XCOM: Enemy Within in November 2013 and a sequel called XCOM 2 in 2016. XCOM: Enemy Unknown was often credited for renewing interest in the turn-based-tactics genre in the 2010s.
